proposed_edges.relationship: McGirr challenges Hofstadter’s psychological characterization of conservatism through the social history of successful modern suburban activists.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own Suburban Warriors introduction, printed 7–8 in the licensed updated-edition publisher excerpt, names Hofstadter’s persecution/paranoid-style interpretation separately from Bell and Lipset’s status-anxiety claims. She credits their attention to ordinary adherents but argues that an excessively psychological framework obscures the Right’s modern social base and durability. This is her attributed historiographical objection, not an independent audit of Hofstadter’s originals, a claim that every conservative was rational, or a denial of conspiratorial rhetoric, which she discusses at 6–10. The introduction’s endnotes are not included in the excerpt and remain unread; no original Hofstadter title is guessed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hartman identifies Du Bois’s formal experimentation as an inspiration for the project that became Wayward Lives.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own Creative Independent interview, originally 18 April 2018 and redisplayed 3 February 2021, answer on teaching Du Bois, explicitly praises the formal variety of The Souls of Black Folk and says his ideas shaped her current project. That project is still described as forthcoming Wayward Lives in this witness. She also retains a critical relation to masculine intellectual self-fashioning and the Philadelphia survey’s pathologizing categories. This positive debt complements, without replacing, edge_1286; neither original Du Bois book nor the complete Hartman monograph is newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hartman explicitly credits Foucault with shaping her understanding of power and discourse while finding limits in his account of domination.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own BOMB 2022 answer to the agency/domination question expressly acknowledges the thinker’s importance to her concepts of knowledge, power and genealogy. Her Venus in Two Acts (2008), 2–3/notes 4–6, 5/note 18 and 10/note 33, also uses Lives of Infamous Men and Archaeology of Knowledge to frame archival visibility and violence. This is a qualified intellectual debt, alongside her separately stated criticism; it is not wholesale adherence or a new reading of Foucault’s originals. Interviewer Jackson’s formulations are distinguished from Hartman’s own acknowledgment.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hartman argues that Foucault’s treatment of extreme domination does not adequately explain racial slavery and enslaved practice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own BOMB 2022 agency answer identifies reading The Ethic of Care alongside The Subject and Power as a turning point: she found no precise account of the domination she needed to analyze, and distinguished enslaved social death from the constrained freedom of a wife. She retains tremendous respect for his thought and says this limit required her to develop an account of her own. This is her retrospective, specific criticism rather than a new independent adjudication of the originals. Her chronology expressly places Scenes before Mbembe’s Necropolitics; no anachronistic claim that the latter caused the 1997 book.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hartman uses de Certeau’s account of historical writing to think about making a place for the living and questioning historical knowledge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own Venus in Two Acts, 14 and note 42, explicitly identifies these two historiographical operations and then reads Octavia Butler’s Kindred as a model for practice along those lines. The note cites The Writing of History in a 1992 manifestation. This resource neither promises recovery of lost lives nor removes Hartman’s insistence on failure and narrative restraint. Butler’s distinct role is retained; neither cited book is newly read, and the citation date is not asserted as first publication.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hartman invokes Scott’s histories of peasant anarchism as a comparative resource for thinking about African and diasporic radical struggle.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own White Review 2020 answer about readers reaching the end of Lose Your Mother explicitly names the political scientist James Scott’s work on South Asian peasants before asking about African resistance to predatory state formations and its diasporic imagination. This is her bounded comparative use, not an assertion that Scott originated African radicalism, a proven personal encounter or a demonstrated cause of her 2007 book. No particular unread Scott title is guessed. Her larger account also credits African writers and other Black traditions that remain explicit missing-endpoint holds.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pocock credits Bailyn, together with Caroline Robbins, with directing him toward commerce’s effects on political thought.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own preface ix expressly identifies both American scholars as showing him the way through commerce before and after 1700 and 1776, then separately credits later Hont and Sonenscher work. This is a plural acknowledged scholarly debt, not formal supervision, sole derivation, or identification of a specific unread Bailyn book. The opposite existing edge_1774 records Bailyn’s use of Pocock; the reciprocal resources are not identical claims. The witness is the publisher preface in a book commonly cited as 2009, whose supplied imprint states 2008.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pocock credits Kuhn’s paradigms with helping him think about the emergence and transformation of political languages, while limiting the analogy.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own preface xi–xiii, notes 10–12, identifies The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), recalls his initial intrigue and gives the post-1688 commercial-society transformation as a useful case. He expressly recognizes an intellectual debt but calls the Kuhnian paradigm a starting point rather than an enduring universal tool. His Oakeshott debt is equally explicit and held for a missing full node. Kuhn’s original and Pocock’s full 1971 essays are unread; a later reported agreement by Kuhn is Pocock’s recollection, not independent correspondence verification.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pocock restricts the transfer of Kuhn’s paradigm revolutions to political history because political communities sustain multiple competing languages.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own preface xii–xiii distinguishes a scientific community of inquiry from political communities exposed to many problems and linguistic alternatives. He allows specific paradigm revolutions but rejects a general requirement that one framework monopolize political discussion. This is a bounded criticism of transferring the model, not a refutation of Kuhn’s account of science. Pocock describes his 1971 essay as self-criticism and says it was less a direct challenge to Kuhn than it appeared; acknowledged influence is retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pocock uses Skinner’s account of what authors were doing as a starting point for tracing readers’ responses and unintended changes in political discourse.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own preface xiv and note 14 explicitly credits Skinner’s 1978 formulation and borrows the language of illocution and allocution while explaining why he pressed toward what authors turned out to have done. This is an acknowledged, critically extended resource, not identical methods or exclusive derivation. The same preface ix distinguishes their research trajectories; existing opposite critique edge_1298 retains its particular 1996 state-concept objection. The Foundations original and the complete 1985 introduction remain unread.
